newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Rebel Cambodia stronghold could soon fall.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Cambodia stronghold could soon fall.

text.p: stronghold of Anlong Veng, once thought to be almost impenetrable, could soon be in government hands for the first time since 1994.
If it did fall, it would not be through force but because rebels once loyal to hated leader Pol Pot appeared to have deserted him, senior military and government officials said.
On Monday, co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh told reporters Pol Pot was on the run east of Anlong Veng after most of his troops had turned their backs on him.
About 95 percent of the Khmer Rouge fighters remaining in Anlong Veng and a group of rebels with Pol Pot wanted to join the government, Ranariddh said.

That would mean Anlong Veng, a 20 km by 100 km (12 mile by 60 mile) area, could soon be under government control for the first time since 1994, when Cambodian forces occupied the base for several weeks, military analysts said.
For years, Anlong Veng has been a primary base of the Khmer Rouge, architects of the 1975-1979 "killing fields" reign of terror in which more than one million people died.

The analysts describe Anlong Veng as a large plain below the Dangrek mountains on the Thai border. While Anlong Veng has large portions of open land with some pockets of jungle, the mountains to the north are covered by deep and rugged jungle. It is also heavily mined.
But the Maoist movement is withering after thousands of defections since last August and the remaining rebels are split over whether to make peace.
The guerrillas have balked at peace before, when they reneged on a 1991 pact meant to end Cambodia's long history of conflict.
They have been fighting a low-intensity war against the coalition government, which was formed after a U.N.-sponsored poll in 1993.

Cambodian officials and military analysts said six rebel divisions remained in Anlong Veng while two more divisions were with Pol Pot. Khmer Rouge divisions are vaguely defined and number anywhere from 50 to 500 soldiers, military analysts said.
"We're not talking about a lot of troops here," a foreign military analyst said.
Not all Anlong Veng's defences are down. Even by the standards of Cambodia, one of the most landmine-ridden countries in the world, Anlong Veng is heavily mined, military analysts said.
"I've seen so many soldiers in the hospitals who have lost arms and legs there. The closer you get (to Anlong Veng), the worse it is," said another military analyst.
If government troops plan to move into Anlong Veng on foot, they will need to find rebels who can identify where the landmines are and lead troops down safe paths, he said.
